
## 7.5-minute recording with a falling heart rate

### Test your predictions using the dataset

The recording comes from an Aidlab chest strap (MIT licence). It lasts 450 s and
contains ECG, beat-to-beat RR intervals, a 5-s pulse signal, respiration,
3-axis acceleration and body position. All timestamps are Unix milliseconds
(UTC). We express time in seconds from the start of the recording
(`from_timestamp_ms` in `dataset.json`).

#### Data import and preparation

We use the **RR intervals** as the main signal, because each interval gives one
heart rate value (HR = 60 000 / RR). This gives about 1 000 points instead of the
91 points of the device's 5-s `pulse` signal. We keep `pulse` as an independent
check. The **acceleration** is used to find out whether the participant is moving.

```{r}
#| label: r7-import

r7_dir <- "data/cardio-recovery-7m30s"
r7_meta <- jsonlite::read_json(file.path(r7_dir, "dataset.json"))
r7_t0 <- r7_meta$from_timestamp_ms

# Beat-to-beat heart rate from RR intervals
r7_rr <- read_csv(file.path(r7_dir, "rr.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t = (timestamp - r7_t0) / 1000,
         rr = value,
         hr = 60000 / rr)

# Device heart rate (one value every ~5 s)
r7_pulse <- read_csv(file.path(r7_dir, "pulse.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t = (timestamp - r7_t0) / 1000, hr = value)

# Movement: SD of the acceleration magnitude in 10-s windows
r7_acc <- read_csv(file.path(r7_dir, "acceleration.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(t = (timestamp - r7_t0) / 1000,
         mag = sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)) |>
  group_by(t = floor(t / 10) * 10 + 5) |>
  summarise(acc_sd = sd(mag), .groups = "drop")

tibble(signal = c("RR intervals", "pulse", "acceleration (10-s windows)"),
       n = c(nrow(r7_rr), nrow(r7_pulse), nrow(r7_acc)),
       t_start_s = c(min(r7_rr$t), min(r7_pulse$t), min(r7_acc$t)),
       t_end_s = c(max(r7_rr$t), max(r7_pulse$t), max(r7_acc$t))) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Signals used in the analysis")
```

Before fitting anything, we check the RR intervals for artefacts (missed or
extra beats). A common rule is to reject any interval that differs by more than
20 % from the previous one.

```{r}
#| label: r7-artefacts

r7_rr <- r7_rr |>
  mutate(rel_change = abs(rr / lag(rr) - 1),
         artefact = !is.na(rel_change) & rel_change > 0.20)

r7_rr |>
  summarise(n_beats = n(),
            n_artefacts = sum(artefact),
            rr_min_ms = min(rr), rr_max_ms = max(rr),
            hr_min_bpm = min(hr), hr_max_bpm = max(hr)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "RR interval quality check")

r7_rr <- filter(r7_rr, !artefact)
```

No interval was rejected, so the RR series is clean. All RR values stay between
368 and 520 ms (115–163 bpm), which is physiologically plausible.

#### Identifying the exercise and recovery periods

```{r}
#| label: fig-r7-overview
#| fig-cap: "7.5-min recording. Top: beat-to-beat HR from RR intervals (grey) and device pulse (black). Bottom: movement (SD of acceleration magnitude, 10-s windows). The dashed line at 330 s marks the moment the participant stops moving."
#| fig-height: 6

r7_t_still <- 330

r7_p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = r7_rr, aes(t, hr), colour = "grey60", size = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = r7_pulse, aes(t, hr), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Heart rate (bpm)") +
  theme_minimal()

r7_p2 <- ggplot(r7_acc, aes(t, acc_sd)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time from start of recording (s)", y = "Acceleration SD (g)") +
  theme_minimal()

patchwork::wrap_plots(r7_p1, r7_p2, ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1))
```

What we observe:

- **No exercise period is visible.** HR is already about 155 bpm in the first
  seconds and starts falling right away. The exercise ended **before** the
  recording started, and we do not know exactly when. So $t = 0$ is the start of
  the recording, not the end of exercise.
- **Fast phase (≈ 0–90 s):** HR drops from about 155 to 131 bpm while the
  participant is moving (acceleration SD ≈ 0.2–0.27 g, a level consistent with
  light activity such as walking).
- **Short pause (≈ 80–100 s):** movement stops briefly (SD ≈ 0.02 g) and HR
  reaches a local minimum (~131 bpm).
- **Plateau (≈ 100–330 s):** movement starts again and HR stays around
  130–137 bpm instead of continuing to fall. This is an **active recovery**.
  The small HR rise around 240–290 s happens while the participant is moving.
- **Rest (≈ 330–450 s):** movement almost stops (SD < 0.07 g) and HR drops
  again, to about 124–130 bpm.
- The body position signal only contains the label `unknown`, so it does not
  help.
  
We therefore consider the **whole recording (0–450 s) as the post-exercise
recovery period**. However, the activity is not constant: it changes from
active to passive recovery at about 330 s. No decay model contains this change,
so we also fit the models on the active part only (0–330 s) as a sensitivity
analysis.

Because $t = 0$ is not the end of exercise, the amplitude of an exponential is
not the true HR drop since the end of exercise. The time constant $\tau$ is not
affected, though: shifting time by $\delta$ in
$a\,e^{-(t+\delta)/\tau}$ only multiplies the amplitude by $e^{-\delta/\tau}$.
Only $\tau$ can be compared with the literature.
#### Fitting the models

We fit the three required models to the beat-to-beat HR:

- **Linear:** $HR(t) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t$
- **Mono-exponential:** $HR(t) = HR_\infty + a\,e^{-t/\tau}$
- **Bi-exponential:** $HR(t) = HR_\infty + a_1 e^{-t/\tau_1} + a_2 e^{-t/\tau_2}$

Non-linear models are fitted by least squares with `nls()`. The bi-exponential
is sensitive to starting values, so we try several and keep the best converged
fit. We use the `port` algorithm with bounds ($a_i \ge 0$, $\tau_i \ge 1$ s).

```{r}
#| label: r7-fit-functions

# Fit a bi-exponential from several starting points and keep the best one
r7_fit_biexp <- function(d) {
  starts <- list(
    list(hr_inf = 125, a1 = 25, tau1 = 40, a2 = 5,  tau2 = 150),
    list(hr_inf = 110, a1 = 25, tau1 = 50, a2 = 25, tau2 = 1000),
    list(hr_inf = 120, a1 = 20, tau1 = 30, a2 = 10, tau2 = 400)
  )
  fits <- map(starts, \(s) tryCatch(
    nls(hr ~ hr_inf + a1 * exp(-t / tau1) + a2 * exp(-t / tau2),
        data = d, start = s, algorithm = "port",
        lower = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 1), upper = c(200, 200, 1e4, 200, 1e5),
        control = list(maxiter = 500)),
    error = function(e) NULL))
  fits <- compact(fits)
  if (length(fits) == 0) return(NULL)
  fits[[which.min(map_dbl(fits, deviance))]]
}

r7_fit_models <- function(d) {
  list(
    linear = lm(hr ~ t, data = d),
    mono = nls(hr ~ hr_inf + a * exp(-t / tau), data = d,
               start = list(hr_inf = 130, a = 25, tau = 40)),
    bi = r7_fit_biexp(d)
  )
}

# Indicators of goodness of fit and residual structure
r7_indicators <- function(models, d) {
  imap(compact(models), \(m, name) {
    e <- resid(m)
    tibble(model = name,
           k = length(coef(m)),
           RMSE = sqrt(mean(e^2)),
           R2 = 1 - sum(e^2) / sum((d$hr - mean(d$hr))^2),
           AIC = AIC(m),
           BIC = BIC(m),
           DW = sum(diff(e)^2) / sum(e^2),        # Durbin-Watson
           acf_lag1 = acf(e, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],
           LjungBox_p = Box.test(e, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")$p.value)
  }) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC), .after = AIC)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: r7-fit-full

r7_models <- r7_fit_models(r7_rr)
r7_ind <- r7_indicators(r7_models, r7_rr)

knitr::kable(r7_ind, digits = c(0, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3),
             caption = "Model comparison on the whole recording (0–450 s, beat-to-beat HR)")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-r7-fits
#| fig-cap: "Linear, mono-exponential and bi-exponential fits to the beat-to-beat heart rate (whole recording)."

r7_grid <- tibble(t = seq(0, max(r7_rr$t), by = 1))
r7_pred <- imap(compact(r7_models), \(m, name)
                mutate(r7_grid, model = name, hr = predict(m, newdata = r7_grid))) |>
  list_rbind()

ggplot(r7_rr, aes(t, hr)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey70", size = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = r7_pred, aes(colour = model), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = r7_t_still, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Time from start of recording (s)", y = "Heart rate (bpm)",
       colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### Fitted parameters

```{r}
#| label: r7-params

r7_param_table <- function(m, name) {
  s <- summary(m)$coefficients
  tibble(model = name, parameter = rownames(s),
         estimate = s[, 1], SE = s[, 2],
         CI_low = s[, 1] - 1.96 * s[, 2],
         CI_high = s[, 1] + 1.96 * s[, 2])
}

imap(compact(r7_models), r7_param_table) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               caption = "Fitted parameters (Wald 95 % CI, whole recording)")
```

- **Linear:** HR falls by `r round(-coef(r7_models$linear)["t"] * 60, 1)`
  bpm/min on average. This model has no physiological meaning: it would predict
  HR to keep falling indefinitely, which is impossible.
  - **Mono-exponential:** $\tau =$ `r round(coef(r7_models$mono)["tau"], 1)` s and
  $HR_\infty =$ `r round(coef(r7_models$mono)["hr_inf"], 1)` bpm. All
  parameters are precise and physiologically interpretable: HR tends towards
  about 131 bpm, the level kept up by the active recovery.
  - **Bi-exponential:** the fast component
  ($\tau_1 \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["tau1"], 1)` s) is plausible,
  but the slow component is **not**:
  $\tau_2 \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["tau2"])` s (more than 2 hours,
  much longer than the 7.5-min recording),
  $a_2 \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["a2"])` bpm, and
  $HR_\infty \approx$ `r round(coef(r7_models$bi)["hr_inf"])` bpm, stuck at the
  lower bound. When $\tau_2 \gg t$, $a_2 e^{-t/\tau_2} \approx a_2 - (a_2/\tau_2)\,t$.
  The "slow exponential" is just a **straight line** with slope
  `r round(-coef(r7_models$bi)["a2"] / coef(r7_models$bi)["tau2"] * 60, 2)`
  bpm/min. $HR_\infty$, $a_2$ and $\tau_2$ cannot be estimated separately (the
  model is not identifiable here), which is also why their standard errors are
  so large.

The data therefore do not contain a second exponential phase within 450 s. What
the bi-exponential captures is a slow downward **drift**, caused mainly by the
end of movement at 330 s. To check this, we fit a more parsimonious model with
the same shape, a **mono-exponential plus a linear drift** (4 parameters instead
of 5):

$$HR(t) = HR_0 + a\,e^{-t/\tau} + b\,t$$


```{r}
#| label: r7-drift

r7_drift <- nls(hr ~ hr0 + a * exp(-t / tau) + b * t, data = r7_rr,
                start = list(hr0 = 130, a = 25, tau = 40, b = 0))

r7_param_table(r7_drift, "mono + drift") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Mono-exponential + linear drift")

r7_indicators(c(compact(r7_models), list(`mono + drift` = r7_drift)), r7_rr) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3),
               caption = "Comparison including the mono-exponential + drift model")
```
